conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for new mothers in the weeks and months after delivery, when emotions can feel like a roller-coaster and everything is changing at once.

To help me understand how things have been going for you, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about your mood, thoughts, and how you’ve been coping over the past seven days. Mothers often tell me it feels like a relief to have their experience put into words, and it helps us decide together what kind of support would be most helpful.

Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise—or unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification whenever you need. When we’re finished, we’ll look at the results privately and talk about next steps that feel right for you.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, I can still laugh—maybe not as easily as before the baby, but if something’s really funny, I’ll catch myself giggling. It just feels a little muted, like I have to remind myself it’s okay to enjoy the moment.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yeah. Like, the other day my partner made a silly joke and I did laugh, but it felt kind of brief—like the smile fades faster than it used to. Most of the time I’m just too tired or distracted to find things funny, even when I know they’re supposed to be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk by myself—but they’re shorter-lived than before. Planning anything feels more like “I guess that could be nice” instead of the bubbly “can’t-wait” feeling I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking, “Maybe I’m not feeding him right,” or, “I must’ve missed some cue.” I know, logically, babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m falling short sometimes.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of times this week I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly worry something’s wrong with the baby—like his breathing sounds off or he feels warm. I check him and he’s fine, so I calm down pretty fast, but those moments still catch me off guard.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not full-on panicky—more like a sudden jolt of “what if something bad happens?” It lasts a minute or two and then fades, but it leaves me feeling on edge for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When the baby’s cluster-feeding and the laundry’s piled up, it feels like I’m drowning in little tasks. I usually get through them, but it’s like I’m running on fumes and every extra request—like the dog needing to go out—makes me want to sit on the floor and cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Not really. I’m tired enough that I can fall asleep okay once the baby settles. I might toss and turn for a bit if I start replaying the day in my head, but I still get a decent stretch most nights.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… I do feel kind of down some days. It’s not constant, but there are moments—especially in the late afternoon—when I just feel heavy and like I could cry for no real reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when the baby wouldn’t nap and once when I dropped a plate and it shattered. It wasn’t about the plate; it just felt like one more thing I couldn’t handle right then.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

Over the past week you've shared that laughter and excitement come only in brief sparks before fading, that worry about your baby's safety jolts you unexpectedly, and that everyday tasks can leave you feeling like you're drowning and ready to sit on the floor and cry. These moments of <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>being overwhelmed</sym> are common but distressing parts of new motherhood, and you showed courage in describing them so openly.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports occasional brief laughter but overall significant reduction in finding things funny, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably diminished anticipation of enjoyable events, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame, mapping to "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes several episodes of sudden, unexplained worry about the baby's health, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, brief fear episodes without clear cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and near-breaking point, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 16 places you above the 14-point cutoff that signals probable <med>postpartum depression</med> requiring urgent follow-up. You endorsed <sym>low mood</sym>, loss of enjoyment, self-reproach, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>crying</sym> most days, aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm thoughts is reassuring, yet the combination of depressive and anxiety symptoms, functional difficulty completing chores, and <quote>running on fumes</quote> warrants immediate evaluation to rule out major depression and begin treatment if indicated. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider or primary care doctor</med> to review these results and consider therapy and/or medication options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive assessment and evidence-based counseling
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track changes after starting supports
4. Share these findings with trusted family so they can help with baby care, meals, or household tasks while you recover
5. Practice 15-20 minutes of gentle outdoor walking or stretching daily; movement can modestly lift mood and reduce <sym>anxiety</sym>
6. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and worry episodes to discuss at your next visit
7. If <sym>panic surges</sym> intensify or you develop any thoughts of self-harm, call 911, go to the nearest emergency department, or contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Screening note – Postpartum visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) interview, patient self-report, 3 wks post-delivery.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (partial) – laughs “briefly,” anticipatory enjoyment “shorter-lived”  
- Daily crying spells, triggered by minor stressors  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt re infant care  
- Recurrent, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety; no compulsions  
- Episodic surges of fear/panic (minutes), resolves spontaneously  
- Feeling “on edge,” “drowning,” easily overwhelmed by routine tasks  
- No sleep-onset problems; occasional early-night rumination  
- Fatigue described as “running on fumes”  
- Denies suicidal ideation, self-harm thoughts, or intent

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms present most days, peaking late afternoon; functional impact moderate (needs support to complete chores, emotional lability).

Screening significance  
EPDS items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 positive; total provisional score suggests elevated risk for postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety. No current safety concerns.

Next steps recommended  
Provide results to PCP/obstetric team; consider formal EPDS scoring, follow-up in 1–2 wks, psychoeducation, support resources; if symptoms escalate or safety issues emerge, expedite mental-health referral.
